{{short description|Polyhedron which tiles 3D space}}

In [[geometry]], a '''space-filling polyhedron''' is a [[polyhedron]] that can be used to fill all of [[three-dimensional space]] via [[translation (geometry)|translation]]s, [[rotation (mathematics)|rotation]]s and/or [[reflection (mathematics)|reflection]]s, where ''filling'' means that; taken together, all the instances of the polyhedron constitute a [[partition of a set|partition]] of three-space. Any [[periodic tiling]] or [[Honeycomb (geometry)|honeycomb]] of three-space can, in fact, be generated by translating a [[primitive cell]] polyhedron.

== Families and their examples ==
If a polygon can tile the plane, its [[Prism (geometry)|prism]] is space-filling; examples include the [[cube]],{{r|erdahl}} [[triangular prism]],{{r|pugh}} and the [[hexagonal prism]].{{r|alexandrov}} Any [[parallelepiped]] tessellates [[Euclidean space|Euclidean 3-space]], as do the five [[parallelohedron|parallelohedra]] (the cube, hexagonal prism, [[truncated octahedron]], [[elongated dodecahedron]], and [[rhombic dodecahedron]]).{{r|alexandrov}} Other space-filling polyhedra include the [[square pyramid]],{{r|barnes}} [[plesiohedron|plesiohedra]],{{r|erdahl}} and [[stereohedron|stereohedra]], polyhedra whose tilings have symmetries taking every tile to every other tile, including the [[gyrobifastigium]],{{r|kepler}} the [[triakis truncated tetrahedron]],{{r|gs}} and the [[trapezo-rhombic dodecahedron]].{{r|lagarias}}

The cube is the only [[Platonic solid]] that can fill space, although a tiling that combines tetrahedra and octahedra (the [[tetrahedral-octahedral honeycomb]]) is possible.{{r|pmtsgsd}} Although the regular tetrahedron cannot fill space, other tetrahedra can, including the [[Goursat tetrahedron|Goursat tetrahedra]] derived from the cube,{{cn|date=January 2026}} and the [[Hill tetrahedron|Hill tetrahedra]].{{r|sv}}

== Characteristics ==
Every polyhedron with [[Dehn invariant]] of zero that can space-fill. Relatedly, two different polyhedra can have Dehn invariants of zero, which may be able to tile each other.{{r|lm}}

== See also ==
* [[Hilbert's eighteenth problem]], one of Hilbert's problems, consisting of three subproblems, one of which is a three-dimensional anisohedral tiling.
* [[Tridecahedron]], a thirteen-sided polyhedron

Voronoi conjectured that all tilings of higher-dimensional spaces by translates of a single [[convex polytope]] are combinatorially equivalent to Voronoi tilings, and Erdahl proves this in the special case of [[zonotope]]s. But as he writes (p.&nbsp;429), Voronoi's conjecture for dimensions at most four was already proven by Delaunay.
